title: TLB Design
summary: The translation cache that makes virtual memory affordable — why translation itself needs caching, and what happens when it misses.

slides.markdown:
The **Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)** is a small, fast cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations. Without it, every single memory access would require a full page-table walk — multiple extra memory reads just to find where the *real* memory read should go.

The TLB turns the common case (translation already cached) into a single fast lookup, which is why virtual memory's overhead is nearly invisible for typical programs despite adding a translation step to every access.

slides.subTitle: The TLB as a cache
slides.markdown:
A page-table walk means one or more extra memory reads (one per level) before the actual data access can even begin. Doing that on *every single* memory access — loads, stores, even instruction fetches — would make virtual memory prohibitively slow.

The TLB exploits the same locality that makes ordinary data caches effective: programs reuse the same handful of pages repeatedly in a short window, so caching their translations captures the vast majority of accesses without ever touching the page table.

slides.subTitle: TLB hit
slides.markdown:
On a **TLB hit**, the CPU finds the needed virtual-to-physical mapping already cached and skips the page-table walk entirely — translation costs essentially nothing extra, adding at most a cycle or two of latency.

Modern CPUs are tuned so that TLB hit rates for typical programs sit well above 95%, which is exactly why virtual memory's translation overhead is rarely visible in everyday performance — the expensive path is the rare one.

slides.subTitle: TLB miss
slides.markdown:
A **TLB miss** means the needed translation isn't cached, so the missing entry must be found via a page-table walk — either performed by a dedicated hardware walker, or (on some architectures) by trapping to a short OS routine that walks the table in software and installs the result into the TLB.

Either way, a TLB miss costs far more than a hit — potentially several extra memory accesses just to resolve the translation before the original access can even proceed.

slides.subTitle: TLB in the access path
slides.markdown:
The TLB sits directly between the CPU and the rest of the memory system, consulted on essentially every load, store, and instruction fetch.

![The TLB positioned between the CPU and the cache/memory system, checked before every access proceeds](assets/tlb-in-access-path.svg)

A hit lets the access proceed immediately with the translated address; a miss detours out to a page-table walk before the original access can complete.

slides.subTitle: TLB reach
slides.markdown:
**TLB reach** is how much memory a TLB can cover without a miss: entries × page size. A TLB with 64 entries and 4KB pages covers only 256KB before it starts missing on a working set bigger than that — surprisingly small compared to typical L2/L3 cache sizes.

This mismatch — data caches routinely much larger than what the TLB can cover — is exactly the motivation for huge pages: covering the same amount of memory with far fewer, larger entries stretches TLB reach dramatically.

slides.subTitle: Hardware-managed vs software-managed TLB
slides.markdown:
| | Hardware-managed (x86) | Software-managed (some RISC/MIPS) |
|---|---|---|
| On a miss | Dedicated hardware walker resolves it | Traps to an OS-defined handler routine |
| Flexibility | Fixed page-table format | OS can define its own table format/policy |
| Miss cost | Lower — no trap overhead | Higher — trap plus handler execution |

Hardware-managed TLBs (x86) resolve misses transparently and fast, but lock in one page-table format. Software-managed TLBs (classic MIPS, some RISC designs) trade a slower miss (a full trap into OS code) for total flexibility in how the OS structures its translation data.

slides.subTitle: Flushing the TLB on every context switch
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Switching processes is cheap, so flushing the TLB every switch is no big deal."

**Why it's wrong:** each process has its own page table, so an entry cached for process A is meaningless (or dangerous) for B. Flushing the *entire* TLB on every switch means the next process pays a burst of misses just rewarming it.

**Correct model:** modern CPUs tag entries with an **ASID** (address-space id), so entries from multiple processes coexist without flushing — hardware ignores entries tagged for a different process.

slides.sectionTitle: The full hit/miss path, end to end
slides.markdown:
Put the whole pipeline together for one load instruction touching virtual address `V`:

```
1. CPU issues load for address V
2. TLB lookup: is V's page present in the TLB?
   HIT  -> physical frame returned in ~1 cycle -> proceed straight to cache access
   MISS -> trigger page-table walk (hardware-page-table-walk): up to 4 sequential
           memory reads on x86-64, each a potential cache miss itself
3. On walk success: install the new translation into the TLB (evicting an entry if full,
   per this topic's replacement policy), then retry the original access — now a TLB hit
4. On walk failure (no valid PTE found): raise a page fault to the OS instead
```

The cost asymmetry is the entire reason TLB design matters: a hit is ~1 cycle, indistinguishable from a normal cache access, while a miss can cost dozens of cycles for the walk alone — before the original memory access even happens. A TLB with a 99% hit rate against a 4-cycle hit / 100-cycle miss still spends `0.01 * 100 = 1` extra cycle per access on average — real, measurable overhead purely from the 1% tail.
